one_line_reason: Multiple meta-analyses and single-ingredient RCTs show oral Amla (Phyllanthus/Emblica officinalis) extract improves lipid/glucose/CRP markers, body composition, and even hair growth in women, with reasonably clear doses in several trials.

selected.population: adults, mostly with elevated cardiometabolic risk factors (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, n=535)
selected.intervention: Emblica officinalis (Amla) fruit, oral, parallel or crossover design
selected.dose_as_stated: 500 mg/day to 1500 mg/day, for 14 to 84 days
selected.why_selected: largest, most rigorous cardiovascular-risk meta-analysis in the shortlist, with a clear dose range and duration.

selected.population: adults, ages roughly 40-58, average BMI ~25.5 (meta-analysis, 5 RCTs)
selected.primary_outcome: CRP, fasting blood glucose, LDL-C, total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL-C
selected.why_selected: second independent meta-analysis corroborating metabolic benefits across a broader marker panel (adds glucose and CRP).

selected.intervention: standardized Amla extract (AMX-160/Tri-Low), oral capsules, 90 days
selected.dose_as_stated: 500 mg once daily or 500 mg twice daily (1 g/day)
selected.primary_outcome: visceral fat, skeletal muscle mass, BMI, waist circumference, lipid profile
selected.why_selected: single-ingredient RCT with a clear, label-mappable dose and a body-composition outcome distinct from the lipid/glucose meta-analyses.

selected.population: women with female androgenetic alopecia (triple-blind RCT, n=60, 52 completers)
selected.why_selected: direct single-ingredient RCT for a common consumer-facing use of Amla (hair health) with a clear oral dose and positive result.

blockers: One selected trial (40262554) uses a specific standardized extract (AMX-160/Tri-Low) that may not match a generic catalog Amla product's extraction method or potency.

Doses vary across trials (500 mg to 1500 mg/day capsule extracts vs. 30 mL/day syrup) with no single consistent standardization (whole fruit powder vs. polyphenol-standardized extract), complicating a single label-dose claim.
The meta-analyses themselves note significant statistical heterogeneity (I2 up to 77%) and urge cautious interpretation of pooled lipid effects.

excluded_pmids.reason: Systematic review of leukoaraiosis severity and endovascular thrombectomy outcomes in stroke; no mention of Amla/Phyllanthus emblica, apparently an unrelated keyword match.

Systematic review of several different herbal medicines (not just Amla) across different COVID-19 trials; Amla's own length-of-stay result is only briefly noted without detail, population is COVID-19 inpatients (a clinical population), and this is redundant with the more detailed, dedicated Amla meta-analyses already selected.
Narrative review of proposed mechanisms for Amla in oral health management; not a quantitative synthesis of clinical trial outcomes.
Narrative mechanistic review of Amla for diabetic complications; does not report pooled human outcome data from trials.

RCT of Amla extract (600 mg) as antitussive premedication during a bronchoscopy procedure; real positive single-ingredient result but a narrow clinical/procedural population and outcome distinct from typical catalog use cases; not selected among the top 4 due to space but worth a follow-up look.
Multi-ingredient liquid nutraceutical (turmeric, pomegranate, amla, ginger, black pepper, niacinamide, CoQ10, folic acid, lycopene); the LDL-lowering effect cannot be attributed to Amla alone.

Primarily a chromium + Phyllanthus emblica + shilajit combination trial; although it includes separate PE-only dose arms (500/1000 mg), the positive effects are reported with mixed significance (p<0.05 to p<0.10) and are harder to cleanly isolate than the dedicated Amla meta-analyses already selected.
Amla extract tested as a topical mouth rinse for halitosis, not a swallowed oral supplement exposure.
